# Differences from the original MSX-AUDIO BASIC extension

> This is an English translation of the [Japanese original](../diff-from-msxaudio.md). Where the two differ, the Japanese version is authoritative.

This document covers only **the differences between MSX-AUDIO BASIC Extension Lite and the original MSX-AUDIO BASIC extension**. For the full specification of the statements and MML, see [`basic-reference.md`](basic-reference.md).

The sound chip it plays is the Y8950, the same as in the original, and **the MML language itself is also almost unchanged from the original**. Most of the differences either come from not having the sound BIOS and the music keyboard, or were added to MML later.

| | |
|---|---|
| [The sound chips and voices are unchanged](#the-sound-chips-and-voices-are-unchanged) | Neither the number of channels nor the order of the strings changes |
| [Statements that were replaced](#statements-that-were-replaced) | Those whose argument form changed |
| [What was added](#what-was-added) | Forms that were originally errors, or did not exist, now have a meaning |
| [What changed](#what-changed) | Written the same way, but takes effect differently |
| [What was removed](#what-was-removed) | Music keyboard, PCM recording, external ROM, two-chip configurations |

When you bring over a program written for the original, **the first thing to fix is the `CALL AUDIO` line**.
Set the second argument (the number of channels for the instrument) to 0, and from there on it usually plays, unless it uses the music keyboard or PCM recording — both the MML and the order of the `PLAY` strings work as they are.

## The sound chips and voices are unchanged

| | Original | This BASIC extension |
|---|---|---|
| Sound chip | MSX-AUDIO (Y8950) | Same. In addition, **the Y8960's extended OPL2 part (OPL2EX)** |
| FM | 9 voices (6 voices when rhythm is used) | Same |
| ADPCM | 1 voice | Same |
| PSG | 3 voices | Same |
| `PLAY` strings | Up to 13 | Same |
| Order of strings and sound chips | FM …, PCM, rhythm, 3 for PSG | Same |
| Channels used by rhythm | 7, 8 and 9 | Same |
| Voice library | 64 voices | **The same 64 voices**. The numbers and names are unchanged, but [the contents are the version in the original MSX-MUSIC BASIC extension](#the-voice-library-and-the-rhythm-voices) |
| ADPCM sample RAM | Depends on the cartridge | Same. 256KB on the Y8960 |

**Channels are used the same way as in the original.** There is no need to reorder the `PLAY` strings of a program written for the original.

In the Y8960 cartridge build only, `PLAY#1` and `PLAY#3` add the 3 voices of the second set of SSGS after the PSG, and there are up to 16 strings ([reference](basic-reference.md#the-six-ssgs-channels-y8960-cartridge-build)).
The order for `#0` and `#2` is unchanged from the original.

Only when running on the Y8960 are [waveform selection](#per-operator-waveform-selection) and panning (`In`) added. Neither form existed in the original MML, so they do not affect how programs written for the original sound.

---

## Statements that were replaced

### CALL AUDIO — initialization arguments

```
CALL AUDIO [([<mode>] [, [0] [, <channels for PLAY string 1>
             [, <channels for PLAY string 2> [, … ]]]])]
CALL AUDIO(-1)
```

| | Original | This BASIC extension |
|---|---|---|
| First argument (mode) | 0-7. bit0 rhythm, bit1 string for PCM, **bit2 CSM mode** | 0-7. bit0 and bit1 are the same, **bit2 selects the interrupt that times note lengths** |
| Second argument | Number of channels for the instrument (music keyboard) | **0 only**. Anything other than 0 gives `Illegal function call` |
| Third argument onward | Number of channels for each string. The total is up to 6 when rhythm is used, 9 when it is not | Same |
| With no arguments | Same as `CALL AUDIO(1,0,2,2,2)` | Same |
| 0 and omission in channel counts | 0 gives `Illegal function call`, omission gives `Syntax error` | Same |
| ADPCM at initialization | The first 32KB of sample RAM as voice file 0 | Same |
| BASIC memory | Not stated in the original documentation | **Decreases by 2051 bytes** (1328 bytes in the Y8960 cartridge build). Variables are also cleared |
| Release | Not possible | **`CALL AUDIO(-1)`** |

**Only the second argument needs fixing.** The channels originally assigned to the music keyboard are either given to `PLAY` instead, or left out.

```basic
CALL AUDIO(1, 2, 1, 2, 1)     ' originally — 2 voices for the instrument
CALL AUDIO(1, 0, 1, 2, 1)     ' now — second argument is 0
```

CSM mode, of which even the original documentation says "Control over all FM sounds (including rhythm sounds) is disabled", does not exist in this BASIC extension. **bit2 has a different meaning** — it selects the interrupt that times note lengths: the screen's vertical sync (0) or the sound chip's timer (1) ([Tempo and the tick source](#tempo-and-the-tick-source)).

### CALL STOPM — takes no argument

Originally, writing `CALL STOPM(<variable name>)` returned in the variable the position at which to resume the stopped MK recording or playback. There is no MK recording, so there is no argument either, and **writing parentheses gives `Syntax error`**. Its function of stopping playback is unchanged from the original.

### CALL VOICE COPY — user voices are 63 to 95

Originally, voice numbers 32-63 were the user voice library in RAM, and transferring into it let you replace all 32 voices with your own. In this BASIC extension, 32-62 remain part of the voice library, which cannot be rewritten, and the user voices are at **63-95**.

| | Original | This BASIC extension |
|---|---|---|
| Voice numbers that can be given as the destination | 32-63 | **63-95** |
| Range of voice numbers | 0-63 | **0-95** |
| Transfer to an array | Possible | Same |
| `*` (all 32 user voices at once) | Can be transferred to and from an array of 1K bytes or more | **Not available** |

```basic
CALL VOICE COPY(A%, @32)   ' accepted originally; now Illegal function call
CALL VOICE COPY(A%, @64)   ' now
```

If a program written for the original used 32-62 for user voices, shifting the numbers to 64-94 lets you rewrite and use them in the same way.

As in the original, each channel can have a different voice, so **the number of voices that can sound at the same time does not decrease.** When there are several voices you want to replace, pass the array variables to `CALL VOICE` as they are.

### CALL SET PCM — devices and sampling frequency

| | Original | This BASIC extension |
|---|---|---|
| Device 0 | External RAM (first channel) | **Sample RAM**. The same thing |
| Devices 1 and 3 | External ROM | **Not available** |
| Device 2 | External RAM (second channel) | **Not available** |
| Device 4 | Main RAM (array variables) | Same |
| Device 5 | VRAM | Same |
| Mode | 0 = ADPCM, 1 = PCM | **0 only**. 1 gives `Illegal function call` |
| Sampling frequency | 1800-16000Hz, default 8000 | **1800-49716Hz**, default 8000 |
| Channel number | 0 or 1 | **0 only** |

**Only voice files on device 0 can be played from MML.** Arrays and VRAM are used as the source and destination of `COPY PCM`. Sounds in arrays or VRAM that were originally played directly by a statement must first be transferred to sample RAM before being played.

### CALL COPY PCM — no built-in voice data

Originally, putting `#` on the source number let you transfer ADPCM built into the system (cuckoo, chicken, dog …) to a voice file. Because there is no sound BIOS, **this form does not exist.**

**Transfers from sample RAM to sample RAM are not possible either** (`Illegal function call`). This is because the sound chip has only 1 address counter; copying is possible by going through an array or VRAM.

How the source and destination are specified, and the unit of offset and length (256 bytes), are unchanged from the original.

## What was added

### MML notation

Forms that were originally errors, or did not exist, now have a meaning.

| Form | Contents | Original |
|---|---|---|
| `Pn` `@Pn` (-1200 to 1200) | Pitch bend. The unit is cents | None |
| `~[n]` | Portamento. Moves smoothly to the next note | None |
| Length `0` (`C0`) | Issues only a note-on and consumes no time | None |
| `R0` | Issues only a note-off and consumes no time | None |
| `R.` | Dotted rest | None |
| `$` followed by 2 hexadecimal digits | `O$04` is `O4`, `Y$30,$53` is `Y48,83` | None |
| `In` (0-255) | Panning. For the FM, PCM and rhythm strings, the Y8960's OPL2EX responds; for the PSG strings, the Y8960's SSGS responds | None |
| Third argument of `Yr, d, m` | Mask of the bits to keep | None |
| `Yr, d` on PSG channels | Writes to PSG registers 0-13. The Y8960 cartridge build also writes SSGS `10H`-`1DH` and `20H`-`2EH` (except `23H` `27H` `2BH`) ([reference](basic-reference.md#the-six-ssgs-channels-y8960-cartridge-build)) | Was ignored |
| `@Vn` on PSG channels (0-128) | In the Y8960 cartridge build, the SSGS channel volume ([reference](basic-reference.md#v-on-psg-channels)). `mabel.rom` accepts it and does nothing | Accepted 0-127 and was ignored |
| `@Wn` on PSG channels | Waits while still sounding | Was the same as `Rn` |
| `{ }n` on PSG channels | Tuplet. Can be written the same as on FM channels | Was `Illegal function call` |

```basic
PLAY#2, "T120O4C0@W8P100@W8P200@W8R0"   ' move the pitch within 1 note
PLAY#2, "O4C4~E4"                       ' rises from C to E over a quarter note
```

**The role of `&` has widened.** As in the original, it joins the notes before and after if they are the same (tie), but when they differ, it replaces only the pitch without issuing key-off / key-on (legato). If a program written for the original has the same note before and after `&`, how it sounds does not change.

### Lengths up to 96

Lengths, originally 1-64, now have an upper limit of **96**. It is the same in all 6 places: `Ln`, `Rn`, `@Wn`, `{ }n`, the length attached to a note, and the length for rhythm.

If you set bit2 of the `CALL AUDIO` mode to time with the sound chip's timer, 96th notes **can be timed exactly at any tempo** ([Tempo and the tick source](#tempo-and-the-tick-source)).

### Per-operator waveform selection

**Offsets 21 and 29** of the voice parameters (reserved in the original) are now waveform selection. Each operator can choose from 4 waveforms.

```basic
CALL AUDREG(&HE0, 1)     ' channel 1 modulator to waveform 1
PLAY#2, "Y$E3,1CDE"      ' channel 1 carrier to waveform 1 as well, then play
```

**It takes effect only on the Y8960's OPL2EX.** An MSX-AUDIO cartridge (Y8950) does not have this register; the write is dropped and the waveform stays a sine wave (it is not an error). All 64 presets of the voice library use waveform 0, so as long as you use the library, it sounds the same on either.

### Releasing with CALL AUDIO(-1)

Originally there was no way to undo initialization. `CALL AUDIO(-1)` stops playback, restores the interrupt hook, returns the memory it took to BASIC, and goes back to the state before `CALL AUDIO` was executed. You can initialize again with `CALL AUDIO`.

The voice file definitions in sample RAM are also lost.

### Statements added in the Y8960 cartridge build

The Y8960 cartridge build has `CALL MUSIC`, `CALL MINIT`, `CALL OPM` and `CALL MIDI`, which switch to the BASIC extension of another sound chip carried on the same cartridge. Before switching, the same cleanup as `CALL AUDIO(-1)` is done automatically.

There is also [`CALL MIXER`](basic-reference.md#call-mixer), which sets the volumes of the cartridge's hardware mixer.

The standalone MSX-AUDIO cartridge build does not have these.

---

## What changed

### Tempo and the tick source

**The tick source can now be selected.** If bit2 of the `CALL AUDIO` mode is 0, it is the screen's vertical sync; if 1, it is the sound chip's timer. **The default is 0**, which corresponds to the same tick source as the original.

When bit2=1, the tick resolution is 48, 96 or 192 per quarter note, decided by the tempo. Real time is determined by the tempo alone, so you need not be aware of it when writing, but the tick rate is rounded to the timer's resolution, so **it deviates by just under 1% from the time the tempo represents** (["Tempo" in `basic-reference.md`](basic-reference.md#tempo)).

**`Tn` is a single value for the whole piece.** Whichever channel it is written on, it changes the tempo of all channels, and the last one read stays in effect. The original documentation does not state whether `T` takes effect per string or for the whole piece.

**The notes that play at the new tempo are those read after the `T`.** Within the same string, it changes from the position where it is written. In the following example, 4 eighth notes play at T120, and then it switches to T240.

```basic
PLAY#2, "T120L8CDEFT240GABC"
```

For notes in other strings, it does not necessarily take effect at that point in the performance. When changing the tempo partway through, write the same `T` in every string, both at the start and at the position where it changes (["Tempo" in `basic-reference.md`](basic-reference.md#tempo)).

With bit2=1, the ticks come from the sound chip's own timer, so **on a machine where the sound chip does not respond, playback does not advance.** `PLAY` returns, but the notes stay in the queue.

### `R` inside a tuplet takes the tuplet length

An `R` with its length omitted inside `{ }` **takes the tuplet length**. `{CDR}4` is 2 twelfth notes and a twelfth rest, fitting into a quarter note. Originally, only the `R` remained a quarter rest, so the tuplet did not fit into a quarter note.

A rest with its length written, as in `{CDR12}4`, does not change. `R` outside a tuplet is also a quarter rest regardless of `Ln`, as in the original.

### `@n` on PSG channels selects tone/noise and the envelope

Originally, `@n` on PSG channels accepted 0-63 and was ignored. It now accepts 0-127 and specifies, in 1 byte, the channel's tone/noise output and the hardware envelope (["`@n` on PSG channels" in `basic-reference.md`](basic-reference.md#n-on-psg-channels)).

| Bit | Contents |
|---|---|
| bit4-0 | When bit4 is 1, hardware envelope, and bit3-0 are its shape (the same as `S`) |
| bit5 | Tone. Sounds at 0 |
| bit6 | Noise. Sounds at 1 |

**If a program written for the original puts `@n` on PSG channels, how it sounds may change.** `@0`-`@31` set that channel to tone only, and `@16`-`@31` select an envelope. `@32`-`@63` stop both tone and noise. An `@n` with bit4 at 0 turns off the envelope, so it takes effect when written after `S`. `@n` on FM channels does not change.

### How PLAY receives its strings

**However many strings made with `+` or functions are lined up in one `PLAY` statement, each one plays as written.** Even when the string area runs short and is reorganized, strings written earlier (including variables) are not corrupted.

```basic
T$="E4"
PLAY#2, "C4"+T$, "D4"+T$    ' 1st plays C E, 2nd plays D E
```

**Built strings are limited to 10 per `PLAY` statement**, and the 11th gives `String formula too complex`. String constants and variables are not counted.

### ADPCM pitch and volume

**The sampling frequency given with `SET PCM` is the reference for pitch.** `O5 E` is the pitch at exactly that frequency, and each semitone away from it multiplies the frequency by 2 to the power of 1/12. The original documentation does not describe the pitch of MML for PCM.

**The volume is set with `Vn` / `@Vn` in the string for PCM.** The original `CALL PCM VOL` does not exist ([What was removed](#what-was-removed)).

### The voice library and the rhythm voices

**The voice library of this BASIC extension follows the version in the original MSX-MUSIC BASIC extension.** The 64 voices come from the library of the original MSX-AUDIO BASIC extension, and some voices were adjusted when ASCII ported it to the OPLL. This BASIC extension carries the adjusted versions.

**The numbers and names are unchanged from the original, but 42 of the 64 voices have different parameters.**
These are `@1` `@7` `@12` `@13` `@15` `@17`-`@22` `@25` `@26` `@32` `@34`-`@47` `@49`-`@62`. The remaining 22 voices are byte-for-byte the same as the original.

Of the 42 voices, 27 differ only in modulation depth, and in many of them the MSX-MUSIC version is milder. The remaining 15 voices also differ in envelope, feedback or transpose. The differences are large in 5 voices: `@7 PipeOrgn`, `@40 PipeOrg2`, `@26 SynRhyth`, `@44 Orch R` and `@50 Magical`. These are better treated as different sounds.

**The rhythm voices are also different from the original.** Instead of the percussion voices that the original sound BIOS had, it uses the OPLL rhythm voices ported to the Y8950's registers. How they are played — `B` `S` `M` `C` `H` and `!`, `Vn`, `@An` — is unchanged from the original; the sounds themselves differ.

### Bits ignored in voice parameters

The 32-byte layout is unchanged from the original, but the following bits are not read.

| Offset | Original | This BASIC extension |
|--:|---|---|
| bit4 of 10 | Fixed pitch | Ignored |
| bit5 of 10 | AMD/PMD loadable | Ignored |
| bit6-7 of 10 | PMD / AMD | Ignored |
| bit4-7 of 20 and 28 | Velocity sensitivity | Ignored |
| bit0-1 of 21 and 29 | (reserved) | **Waveform selection** (OPL2EX only) |

bit0-3 of offset 10 (algorithm and feedback) and the operator parameters at 16-19 and 24-27 are unchanged from the original.

### Arguments for two-chip configurations

Configurations with 2 MSX-AUDIO LSIs are not supported. How an argument that refers to the second channel is handled depends on the statement.

| | Original | This BASIC extension |
|---|---|---|
| Third argument of `CALL AUDREG` | 0 or 1 | **0 or omitted**. 1 gives `Illegal function call` |
| Second argument of `CALL PITCH` | Pitch of the second channel | **Ignored** |
| Second argument of `CALL TRANSPOSE` | Transpose of the second channel | **Ignored** |
| `CALL VOICE` | Sets the same voice on both channels | For 1 chip only |

### MIDI

MIDI output, which was an option in the original, does not exist.

| | Original | This BASIC extension |
|---|---|---|
| `PLAY #1` | Outputs performance data to the MIDI port | `Illegal function call`. In the Y8960 cartridge build, PSG and the second set of SSGS ([reference](basic-reference.md#the-six-ssgs-channels-y8960-cartridge-build)) |
| `Zd` | Sends data d to MIDI | `Illegal function call` (ignored in strings for PSG) |

## What was removed

**The statements are kept by name only, and writing them after `CALL AUDIO` has initialized the system gives `Illegal function call`** (before initialization, `Syntax error`). A program written for the original stops at that line, so you can tell where it used them. Things removed as arguments or device numbers give an error when that value is written (the parentheses of `CALL STOPM` give `Syntax error`).

| | |
|---|---|
| **Music keyboard (instrument)** | `CALL INMK` `CALL KEY ON` `CALL KEY OFF` `CALL MK PCM` `CALL MK TEMPO` `CALL MK VEL` `CALL MK VOICE` `CALL MK VOL`. The second argument of `CALL AUDIO` also belongs here |
| **MK recording** | `CALL APPEND MK` `CALL CONT MK` `CALL MK STAT` `CALL PLAY MK` `CALL REC MK` `CALL RECMOD`. The argument of `CALL STOPM` also belongs here |
| **MSX-AUDIO system memory and applications** | `CALL APEEK` `CALL APOKE` `CALL SYNTHE` |
| **Disk I/O** | `CALL LOAD PCM` `CALL SAVE PCM`. Read and write an array with `BSAVE` / `BLOAD` of standard BASIC, and pass it to sample RAM with `COPY PCM` |
| **Recording and format conversion** | `CALL REC PCM` `CALL CONVA` `CALL CONVP`. Only ADPCM is handled now |
| **Playback from statements** | `CALL PLAY PCM` `CALL PCM FREQ` `CALL PCM VOL`. ADPCM is played from the string for PCM in `PLAY` |
| **Voice files in external ROM** | Devices 1 and 3 of `SET PCM`, and ROM voice file numbers |
| **Built-in ADPCM voice data** | Source numbers with `#` in `COPY PCM` |
| **Two-chip configurations** | Devices 2 and 3 of `SET PCM`, and the second channel of each statement |
| **CSM mode** | bit2 of the `CALL AUDIO` mode (used with a different meaning) |
| **MIDI** | `PLAY #1` and `Zd` |
| **32-62 of the user voice library** | 32-62 cannot be rewritten. User voices are 63-95 |

---

## What has not changed

MML, including that for rhythm, can be used as it is.

- Notes, rests, octaves, `Mn`, `Sn`, `Vn`, `Qn`, `Nn`, `.`
- `{ }n` ([only the length of the `R` inside has changed](#r-inside-a-tuplet-takes-the-tuplet-length))
- `@n` on FM channels (0-63; [user voices 64-95](#call-voice-copy--user-voices-are-63-to-95) are added as well), `@Vn` (0-127), `Yr, d`, `=x;`, `Xx;`
- `Tn` range 32-255, `On` range 1-8, `Nn` range 0-96
- MML for rhythm sounds (`B` `S` `M` `C` `H` `!` `Vn` `@An` and lengths)
- `#0` of `PLAY` is compatible with the conventional PSG PLAY

Apart from the differences listed above, statements also keep the same names and arguments.

- `CALL BGM`, `CALL PLAY`, `CALL VOICE`, `CALL AUDREG`
- `CALL PITCH` (410-459), `CALL TRANSPOSE` (±12799), `CALL TEMPER` (0-21)
- The numbers and names of the 64 voices in the voice library ([the contents of 42 voices differ](#the-voice-library-and-the-rhythm-voices))
- The 32-byte layout of the voice parameters

**Just intonations 11-21 of `CALL TEMPER` run through the keys in the reverse order of the table in the original documentation.** The original documentation gives 11 as cis major and 21 as h major, but what this BASIC extension plays is h major for 11 and cis major for 21 ([table](basic-reference.md#call-temper)).
